plural-forms.intro_tr: In Dutch, the plural of nouns is formed with two main suffixes: -en (the most common) and -s. Which suffix is used depends on the stress of the final syllable of the word, the final letter, and sometimes established conventions; therefore there are many exceptions that require memorization. When the -en suffix is added, spelling changes frequently occur (vowel lengthening/shortening, consonant doubling, s→z or f→v transformation). Additionally, completely irregular plurals such as het kind → kinderen, de stad → steden also exist. This page is a comprehensive reference that collects the rules and exceptions in one place.

present-tense.intro_tr: In Dutch, the present tense (tegenwoordige tijd) serves both the function of the present tense in Turkish and the general/habitual tense: it is used both to mean "is happening now" and "happens in general/always". Conjugation is done by adding -t or -en endings to the verb's "stam" (stem/root) according to the person; there is no separate ending like "-iyor". When finding the root, certain spelling rules (vowel doubling, consonant gemination) come into play. When the "jij" subject comes AFTER the verb (as in questions), the -t letter in the conjugation ending drops; this is an important rule specific to Dutch. Verbs like zijn, hebben, gaan, doen are common and irregular and must be memorized separately.

question-formation.intro_tr: In Dutch, question sentences are formed using two main methods: Yes/No questions and questions formed with question words (wie, wat, waar, wanneer...). In Yes/No questions, the subject-verb order in a regular sentence is reversed; the conjugated verb comes to the beginning of the sentence, the subject immediately follows it (Verb + Subject). In questions with question words, the sentence begins with the question word and due to the V2 rule, the conjugated verb is in the second position. If the object being asked about is an inanimate thing using 'wat' and will be used with a preposition, combined question words like "waarmee" are preferred instead of "met wat" (waar+preposition). On this page all question words, conjugation and inversion examples, combined question words and the use of welke/welk are summarized in table form.

personal-pronouns.intro_tr: Dutch personal pronouns are examined in three main groups according to their functions in the sentence: subject (onderwerp), object (object), and possessive (bezittelijk), and each group has its own full form (volle vorm) and unstressed/short form (verzwakte vorm). In spoken language, short forms (je, ze, 'm, m'n, etc.) are generally used, while in written language and when emphasis is desired, full forms (jij, haar, mijn) are preferred. Additionally, the distinction by gender (hij/zij/het), the distinction by formality (jij/u), and the existence of two different pronouns in plural third person object use (hen/hun) are different from Turkish and are the most difficult points for Turkish students. On this page, all pronoun tables, short/long form distinctions, and hen-hun-ze usage rules are collected in a single reference.

adjective-inflection.intro_tr: In Dutch, when an adjective is used BEFORE a noun (attributief / attributive position), it most often takes an -e suffix at the end: for example "groot" (big) → "grote auto". Whether this -e suffix is added depends on whether the noun is a de-woord or het-woord, whether it is singular or plural, and whether the article is definite (de/het/deze/die) or indefinite (een). By contrast, when an adjective is used AFTER verbs like "zijn", "worden", "lijken" in PREDICATE position, it NEVER takes -e. When adding the suffix, certain spelling (vowel/consonant) changes come into play, and also adjectives denoting material and ending in -en (such as houten, gouden) always remain unchanged. This page brings together all the -e inflection rules and exceptions most frequently encountered at N5 level in one place.

modal-verbs.title_tr: Modal Verbs (kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen, zullen)
modal-verbs.intro_tr: In Dutch, modal verbs (modale werkwoorden) are used to express the ability to perform an action, necessity, desire, permission, or possibility. The five most commonly used modal verbs are: kunnen (to be able to), moeten (to have to/must), willen (to want), mogen (to be allowed/may) and zullen (future/to indicate suggestion). A modal verb is positioned in the second place in the sentence (V2 rule) and is conjugated according to the subject, while the main verb remains in the infinitive (infinitief) form and goes to the END of the sentence. When creating negatives, instead of "moeten + niet", generally "hoeven te + niet" is used, which is the closest structure to the meaning of "doesn't need to" in Turkish. On this page you will find the conjugations of the five modal verbs in present tense and past tense (imperfectum), their meanings, and their uses within sentences in table form.

de-het-articles.intro_tr: Dutch nouns have a "grammatical gender" that does not exist in Turkish: each noun belongs to either the "de-woord" (masculine/feminine) or "het-woord" (neuter) group, and this determines whether the definite article will be "de" or "het". Approximately 75% of nouns take "de", 25% take "het"; there is no fixed phonetic rule that shows this distribution, which is why each new word must be memorized together with its article. Nevertheless, there are some reliable clues: ALL plural nouns take "de", ALL diminished nouns (with the -je suffix) take "het", and certain word endings/categories largely point to one article. The indefinite article (meaning "a") is the same for both de- and het-words: "een". This page presents category and suffix tables together that will facilitate the choice of article.

negation-niet-geen.intro_tr: In Dutch, two different words are used to form negative sentences: "niet" and "geen". Which one is chosen depends on the type of the element being negated: "geen" negates only indefinite nouns (singular nouns used with 'een', plural nouns, and uncountable nouns); "niet" is used for verbs, adjectives, adverbs, prepositional phrases, and definite nouns (those used with 'de'/'het'/possessives). The position of "niet" in the sentence is not fixed; it changes depending on the element it negates, and this is usually the most confusing part for Turkish students. This page clarifies with tables which word to use in which situation and where.

footnotes_tr: Rule summary: if there's 'een' before the noun or if the noun is plural/uncountable and indefinite → geen. In all other cases → niet.

footnotes_tr: General tendency: niet comes IMMEDIATELY BEFORE the element it negates; but in simple verb negation it goes at the end of the sentence.
In sentences with comparison/emphasis, niet can also come before the emphasized element: Ik ga niet vandaag, maar morgen.

zijn-hebben.intro_tr: In Dutch, "zijn" (to be) and "hebben" (to have/possess), like "to be" and "to have" in English, are irregular but most frequently used two basic verbs. These verbs both carry meaning on their own and are also used as auxiliary verbs together with other verbs in past tense (perfectum) sentences — therefore, memorizing their conjugations is the foundation of learning Dutch. Unlike Turkish, many expressions such as "I'm hungry", "I'm cold", "How old am I" are formed in Dutch with hebben or zijn, so special attention should be paid to idiomatic expressions. In the tables below, present tense, past tense (imperfectum), perfectum conjugations, and auxiliary verb usage rules are fully provided.

'u', as both a singular and plural polite pronoun, takes the same verb form: u bent, u heeft/hebt.

word-order-v2.intro_tr: The most basic and most frequently violated rule of Flemish (Dutch) is the V2 (Verb-Second) rule: in MAIN clauses, the conjugated (conjugated according to person) verb is always in the position of the 2nd element of the sentence — whether it's the subject, adverb, object, or subordinate clause at the beginning of the sentence makes no difference. If there is something other than the subject at the beginning of the sentence (for example, a temporal adverb), the subject moves AFTER the verb; this is called "inverted structure" (inversie). In compound tenses (perfectum, future tense, modal verbs, separable verbs), only the auxiliary/modal verb remains in the 2nd position, and the main verb or separable particle goes to the END of the clause. In subordinate clauses (those starting with conjunctions like omdat, als, dat) the V2 rule does not apply — the verb is placed at the end of the clause. Understanding this rule well is the key to forming natural and correct Flemish sentences.

tables.caption_tr: The Basic Logic of the V2 Rule: The Verb Always in the 2nd Position
footnotes_tr: Rule: No matter WHAT in the sentence (subject, adverb, object, subordinate clause), the conjugated verb is always the 2nd element — meaning the 2nd ELEMENT/GROUP, not the 2nd WORD.
'Naar school' is counted as a single element (group), so the verb comes in the 2nd position after the entire element, not after 'naar' but after 'school'.

tables.caption_tr: Inverted Structure (Inversie): The Subject Shifts After the Verb
rows: Ik vind dit een goed idee.
Dit vind ik een goed idee.
footnotes_tr: In inverted structure, the subject comes IMMEDIATELY AFTER the conjugated verb; no other element can come in between.
This structure is unusual compared to Turkish word order because in Turkish the verb is always at the end; in Flemish the verb's position is fixed, the subject moves.

tables.caption_tr: V2 in Compound Tenses: Auxiliary/Modal Verb in 2nd Position, Main Verb or Particle at the End
rows: Het huis wordt volgend jaar verkocht.
footnotes_tr: This 'splitting' structure is called a 'verb frame', like in German (werkwoordelijke eindgroep): the middle of the sentence is surrounded by verbs.
In separable verbs, the prefix (op, aan, mee, terug vb.) always goes to the very end of the sentence, while the conjugated part remains in the 2nd position.

pronunciation-spelling.title_tr: Pronunciation and Spelling (ij, ui, g sound)
pronunciation-spelling.intro_tr: Dutch spelling, unlike Turkish, contains many special vowel/diphthong sounds (ij, ei, ui, ou, eu, oe) and a guttural "g/ch" sound; these sounds have no direct equivalents in Turkish and require practice for correct pronunciation. Additionally, the foundation of Dutch spelling lies in the "open/closed syllable" rule: this rule determines when a vowel should be written with a single letter, when with a doubled letter (aa, ee, oo, uu), and when a consonant should be doubled when a suffix is added to a word (kat→katten). Voiced consonants like d, b, v, z at the end of words harden and are pronounced like t, p, f, s, but when an inflective suffix is added, the original sound returns (huis→huizen). The IJ letter in the Dutch alphabet acts as a single unit, and at the beginning of a sentence/proper noun, both letters are capitalized (IJsselmeer). This page summarizes the most frequently encountered pronunciation and spelling rules at the N5 level in table format.

future-tense.intro_tr: In Dutch, the future tense is constructed with two basic auxiliary verbs: "gaan" and "zullen". "Gaan" is the most frequently used way in everyday conversation and is generally preferred for near-future events that are pre-planned, decided, or evidence-based (e.g., looking at clouds and saying "it will rain"). "Zullen" is used more for uncertain predictions, making promises, making offers, making spontaneous decisions, and in formal/written language. Both verbs are conjugated and the infinitive form of the main verb is added to the end of the sentence: Subject + gaan/zullen (conjugated) + ... + infinitive. This structure corresponds to the "-ecek/-acak" future tense suffix in Turkish, but which verb is chosen in Dutch depends on the context.

subordinate-clauses.title_tr: Subordinate Clauses and Verb Final Position
subordinate-clauses.intro_tr: In Dutch, sentences are divided into two types: "hoofdzin" (main clause) and "bijzin" (subordinate clause). In the main clause, the verb is always in the second element position (V2 rule), but in subordinate clauses beginning with a conjunction like "omdat, dat, als, terwijl", the conjugated verb (and any auxiliary/modal verbs if present) goes to the end of the sentence — this is called "fiil sona atma" (werkwoord op het einde). This is an important rule specific to Dutch, different from English and Turkish, and when forgotten, the sentence sounds incorrect/strange. If the subordinate clause comes before the main clause, the subject-verb positions in the main clause swap (inversion/devrik yapı). In the tables below, you can see which conjunctions trigger this rule and how complex verb groups (perfectum, modal verbs) are ordered in the subordinate clause.

separable-verbs.intro_tr: Separable verbs (scheidbare werkwoorden) consist of a combination of a prefix (aan, op, uit, mee, weg etc.) with a base verb; even though they are written as a single word in the dictionary (opbellen, aankomen), in main clauses the prefix separates from the verb and goes to the very end of the sentence. For example, the verb "opbellen" (to call) is used as "Ik bel mijn moeder op." Because this structure is very different from compound verbs in Turkish, it is necessary to memorize the prefix list, its conjugation form, and its position according to sentence type. When forming Perfectum (present perfect tense), the "ge-" suffix enters between the prefix and the verb root (opgebeld). With modal verbs and in subordinate clauses, the prefix and verb are used together without separating.

comparatives.intro_tr: In Hollandaca, the comparative degree (comparatief) of adjectives is formed with -er, and the superlative degree (superlatief) is formed with de/het + adjective + -st suffix; the system is very similar to the -er/-est structure in English and quite regular. In short, single-syllable adjectives, some spelling rules such as consonant doubling or vowel shortening come into play. To say "X is more ... than Y", the word dan is used, and to say "X is as ... as Y", even/net zo...als is used. A few frequently used adjectives/adverbs like goed, veel, weinig and graag are irregular and must be learned by heart. The superlative can be used both as an adjective before the noun and as an adverb after the verb (het + -st).

diminutives.intro_tr: In Dutch, to 'diminish' a noun, a variant of the -je suffix is added to its end; this is called 'verkleinwoord' (diminutive noun). This suffix not only expresses physical smallness, but can also add emotional tones such as affection/tenderness, politeness, or trivialization. Which suffix variant (-je, -tje, -pje, -kje, -etje) is used depends entirely on the final letters of the word and the structure of its final syllable. A diminutive noun, regardless of the gender of the original word, ALWAYS takes the article 'het' and its plural is always formed regularly with the -s suffix. Some words, however, only exist in diminutive form or acquire a completely different/independent meaning when combined with the diminutive suffix.

imperfect-tense.intro_tr: Imperfectum (narrative past tense) is the simple past tense used in Dutch to describe actions that happened, were completed, or became habitual in the past — it serves a function similar to the Turkish "-dı/-di" suffix. For regular verbs, -te(n) or -de(n) is added to the root end according to the 't kofschip' rule. Irregular (strong) verbs have their own specific imperfectum forms that must be memorized. In everyday speech, Dutch speakers generally prefer perfectum (hebben/zijn + participle); imperfectum is more common in written language, narrative contexts, and with frequently used verbs like zijn, hebben, kunnen. On this page you will find the rules, complete conjugation tables, and the most commonly used irregular verbs.

tables.caption_tr: Regular verb conjugation rule: 't kofschip (hard/soft consonant rule)
rows: t, k, f, s, ch, p ('t kofschip / 'x-tje kaf' harfleri)
Diğer tüm ünsüzler ve sesli harfler (yumuşak)
footnotes_tr: Rule: find the root of the infinitive (werken → werk), if the last letter of the root is one of the 't kofschip' letters (t,k,f,s,ch,p) add -te/-ten, otherwise add -de/-den.
If the root already ends in -t or -d, no extra letter is added but the suffix still follows the rule: praten → praatte (root 'praat' + te), antwoorden → antwoordde.

tables.caption_tr: Complete conjugation table: werken ('t kofschip → -te) and wonen (soft → -de)
footnotes_tr: Singular forms (ik, jij/u, hij/zij/het) are always identical to each other; in the plural, only -n is added at the end.
This dual pattern applies to all regular verbs — only the choice of -te(n)/-de(n) changes according to the root letter.

tables.caption_tr: Semi-irregular verbs: root '-cht-' change (must be memorized)

footnotes_tr: In strong verbs, the root vowel typically changes (i→e, ee→a, etc.) and the -te(n)/-de(n) suffix is not added; these forms must be memorized individually.
In most strong verbs, the plural form is obtained by adding only -en to the singular form (e.g. ging → gingen), but in some the root also changes (nam → namen).

The 'wou' form of the verb 'willen' is also common in spoken language; in written language 'wilde' is preferred.

er-usage.intro_tr: "Er" is a versatile, small but indispensable word in Hollandaca that cannot be fully translated into Turkish. It has five basic uses: indicating existence ("var" meaning), pointing to a previously mentioned place ("there"), referring to inanimate objects with prepositions (er + preposition), representing the object in number/quantity expressions, and serving as a dummy subject in subjectless/passive sentences. Because there is no equivalent in Turkish, students often omit this word, but for correct and natural Hollandaca, "er" is often mandatory. On this page, you will examine all uses of "er", preposition combinations, and its position in the sentence with tables.

possessives-genitive.intro_tr: In Dutch, there are three main ways to express possession: possessive pronouns (mijn, jouw, zijn, haar, ons/onze, jullie, hun), -s genitive used with proper nouns (Jans boek = Jan's book), and the van structure that can be used with every noun (het boek van Jan). In spoken language, the van structure is much more common; -s genitive is seen mostly in written language and with personal names. The ons/onze distinction depends on the de/het rule and is frequently confused. Whether an apostrophe is used in the -s genitive depends on the last letter of the noun, which requires attention in spelling.

adverb-formation.intro_tr: In Dutch, degree modifiers such as heel, erg, nogal, tamelijk, vrij, behoorlijk, zeer are used to intensify the degree of an adjective or modifier; these correspond to words in Turkish like çok, oldukça, epey, hayli. These modifiers are always placed immediately before the adjective or modifier they intensify and do not undergo conjugation themselves. The difference between them is mostly in semantic degree (light–strong) and register (everyday speech – formal written language); some (like nogal) can also carry a slight surprise or negative connotation. heel can also be used with nouns in the sense of "whole, entire" and in this case requires a different structure (heel de stad / een hele dag). On this page you will find in table form the most commonly used degree modifiers, the special uses of heel, and common mistakes.

aan-het-progressive.title_tr: Continuous: aan het + Infinitive, zitten/staan te
aan-het-progressive.intro_tr: Dutch does not have a separate grammatical tense called 'present continuous' (present continuous) as in English; however, to emphasize that an action is happening at that exact moment, continuously, two constructions are used: 'zijn + aan het + infinitive' and the construction with posture verbs 'zitten/staan/liggen/lopen + te + infinitive'. These constructions are not mandatory — Dutch present tense (presens) can already express both habit and instantaneous action — but they are preferred when wanting to particularly emphasize the continuous nature. The 'aan het' construction is neutral and can be used with almost any verb, while the posture verb construction also indicates that the subject is physically sitting, standing, lying, or moving at that moment, which is why it is more colorful and descriptive in spoken language. Both constructions are easily inflected with present tense (presens) and past tense (imperfectum).

tables.caption_tr: 1. Formation of 'aan het + infinitive' construction according to tenses
rows: Ik ben aan het werken geweest.
Ik zal aan het werken zijn.
footnotes_tr: The 'aan het' construction is formed only with the auxiliary verb 'zijn', not with 'hebben'.
The infinitive (infinitief) always remains unchanged at the end of the sentence.

tables.caption_tr: 2. Full conjugation of 'zijn + aan het + infinitive' (example verb: werken)
3. Posture verbs: zitten / staan / liggen / lopen + te + infinitive

özne hareket halindeyken veya tekrarlayan eylemlerde
footnotes_tr: The posture verb is chosen according to the subject's actual physical position; therefore, it is not used with every verb, but with verbs that make sense.

tables.caption_tr: 4. Full conjugation of 'zitten te + infinitive' (example verb: praten)

tables.caption_tr: 5. Present and imperfect conjugations of the verbs staan, liggen, lopen

relative-clauses.intro_tr: In Dutch, relative (participial) clauses are used to qualify a noun with another clause, and they are equivalent to the Turkish "...an/-en" participle structures, but in Dutch they are formed as an independent subordinate clause, placed immediately after the noun, separated by a comma. Which relative pronoun is used depends on whether the qualified noun is a de-woord or het-woord and whether it is singular or plural: die and dat. When used together with a preposition for objects and places, the waar+preposition (waarin, waarop, waarmee...) form is preferred instead of die/dat; for people, preposition+wie (met wie, voor wie) is used. In the relative clause, the verb is always moved to the end, because this is a subordinate clause. This page summarizes the die/dat/waar choice and frequently confused points with tables.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Rule: die or dat?
rows: de man die... / de auto die...
het boek dat... / het huis dat...
de boeken die... / de huizen die...
footnotes_tr: In plural, even if it is het-woord, the difference disappears: always 'die' is used.
The relative pronoun is chosen based on the gender of the qualified noun, not based on the function of the subject or object.

tables.caption_tr: For Objects/Concepts: waar + Preposition
footnotes_tr: The waar+preposition structure is used when the qualified noun is a place, object, or abstract concept (if not a person).
'die/dat + preposition' (e.g. de pen die ik mee schrijf) is sometimes heard in everyday speech, but the correct form in written language is waar+preposition.

tables.caption_tr: For People: Preposition + wie
rows: De vrouw met wie ik praat...
De persoon voor wie ik werk...
De man aan wie ik het gaf...
De vriend van wie ik dit hoorde...
De familie bij wie ik logeer...
De collega over wie we praten...
footnotes_tr: For people, 'waar+preposition' is never used; only preposition+wie is correct.
In a non-prepositional context, the normal 'die' is used for people: de man die ik ken.

tables.caption_tr: wat Usage Cases

Belirsiz zamirlerden sonra die/dat değil wat kullanılır.

Önceki tüm cümleyi (tek bir ismi değil) niteleyen yan cümlelerde wat kullanılır.
footnotes_tr: In cases where wat is used, when combined with a preposition, 'waar' is used: alles waar ik aan denk (not: alles wat ik aan denk).

om-te-infinitive.title_tr: "om ... te + Infinitive" Structures — Purpose-Indicating Verb Patterns
om-te-infinitive.intro_tr: The "om ... te + infinitive" structure in Dutch is used to express the PURPOSE of an action and corresponds to the Turkish suffix "-mek için" (in order to). In this structure, "om" appears in the continuation of the main clause, while the infinitive (infinitief) appears at the very end of the clause together with "te"; the space between "om" and "te" can be filled with other elements such as object, adverb, etc. Note: The plain "te + infinitive" structure used without "om" comes as a MANDATORY complement after certain verbs such as proberen, beginnen, hopen, vergeten, and expresses not purpose but the structure required by that verb. After modal verbs (kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen, zullen) and verbs like gaan, komen, blijven, laten, zien, horen, "te" is not used at all — the bare infinitive is used. Negative purpose clauses are constructed with the pattern "om niet te" or "om geen ... te".

tables.caption_tr: Basic Schema of the "om ... te" Structure
rows: Ik leer Nederlands om te werken.
Ana cümle + om + nesne + te + mastar
Ik leer Nederlands om een baan te vinden.
Ana cümle + om + zarf + te + mastar
Hij komt vroeg om op tijd te zijn.
Ana cümle + om + nesne + zarf + te + mastar
Ze belt hem elke dag om hem te steunen.
Onu desteklemek için her gün onu arıyor.
Om gezond te blijven, sport ik veel.
Sağlıklı kalmak için çok spor yapıyorum.
footnotes_tr: If the "om" phrase is placed at the beginning of the sentence, it is separated from the main clause by a comma.
Everything between om and te is the infinitive's own complement (object, adverb, prepositional phrase, etc.).

tables.caption_tr: The Difference Between "om te" and Plain "te"
rows: AMAÇ bildirir — "niçin/ne amaçla?" sorusuna cevap verir
Ik werk om geld te verdienen.
Belirli fiillerden sonra zorunlu tümleç; amaç bildirmez
"om" sadece amaç varsa kullanılır, proberen/beginnen gibi fiillerle KULLANILMAZ
✗ Ik probeer om te slapen. (günlük konuşmada duyulsa da yazı dilinde hatalı sayılır)
footnotes_tr: In colloquial speech, 'om' is sometimes added unnecessarily, but in written/formal Dutch this is considered incorrect.

tables.caption_tr: Common Verbs Requiring "te + Infinitive" (WITHOUT om)
rows: Ik hoop je snel te zien.
footnotes_tr: All of these verbs take 'te + infinitive' directly as their own complement; 'om' is not placed between them.

tables.caption_tr: Verbs NOT Requiring "te" (Bare Infinitive)
rows: Oturmuş okuyor. (bu yapıda 'te' vardır ama 'om' asla yoktur)
footnotes_tr: Posture verbs actually take 'te' but 'om' is never used; this is a separate continuous structure (see zitten/staan te).

tables.caption_tr: Negative Purpose: "om niet te" / "om geen ... te"
rows: Ze fluistert om het kind niet wakker te maken.
Hij rijdt langzaam om geen ongeluk te veroorzaken.
Hij schrijft alles op om nooit iets te vergeten.
Hiçbir şeyi asla unutmamak için her şeyi not ediyor.
footnotes_tr: The negation word (niet/geen/nooit) always appears immediately before the infinitive, also before 'te'.

tables.caption_tr: Use of "om te" with Separable Verbs
rows: Ik gebruik mijn telefoon om je op te bellen.
Ze pakt een tas om haar boeken mee te nemen.
Kitaplarını götürmek için bir çanta alıyor.
Hij gaat naar het ziekenhuis om zijn vader op te zoeken.
Babasını ziyaret etmek için hastaneye gidiyor.
Ze werkt laat om de presentatie voor te bereiden.
Sunumu hazırlamak için geç saatlere kadar çalışıyor.
footnotes_tr: In separable verbs, 'te' is inserted BETWEEN the prefix and verb root: op + te + bellen → op te bellen.

passive-voice.intro_tr: In Dutch, the passive voice is constructed with the auxiliary verb "worden" + past participle (voltooid deelwoord) when the object affected by the action is intended to be highlighted instead of the person performing the action. It corresponds to the passive suffix "-il, -in, -l" in Turkish: like "yazılıyor, yazıldı, yazılacak". When the agent needs to be specified, the prepositions "door" (by whom) or "met" (with what) are used. An important detail: in the near past and earlier times, the auxiliary verb "zijn" is used instead of "worden" and the full form "geworden" is practically dropped. "Worden + participle" narrates an action/process, while "zijn + participle" mostly narrates a finished state; these two are the most frequently confused points at B1 level.

tables.caption_tr: Complete Conjugation of the Verb worden (Present and Past Tense)

tables.caption_tr: Formation of Passive Voice According to Tenses

fixed-prepositions.intro_tr: In Dutch, many verbs are used in a fixed manner with a certain preposition, and this preposition may not have a one-to-one correspondence with its Turkish equivalent (e.g., "wachten OP" = "to wait for", the preposition cannot be guessed from the word's meaning). These structures are called "vaste voorzetsels" (fixed prepositions) and must be memorized, because they are learned as fixed phrases rather than through logic. After this preposition + verb pair, generally comes a noun, person, or subordinate clause (dat/of clause or om te + infinitive). When asking questions, "waar + preposition" (waarop, waarover) is used for inanimate objects, and "preposition + wie" (op wie, aan wie) for animate objects; when referring or pointing, "er + preposition" (erop, eraan) forms come into play. This page presents the most frequently used verb-preposition combinations and their pitfalls in table form.

reflexive-verbs.intro_tr: In Dutch, reflexive verbs (wederkerende werkwoorden) are verbs that use the reflexive pronoun "zich" (oneself) to indicate that the subject performs the action on itself; like "myself, yourself" in English, but in Dutch the pronoun changes according to the person (me, je, zich, ons, je, zich). Some verbs are always reflexive and make no sense without a pronoun (zich vergissen — to be mistaken), while others can be used both reflexively and transitively (wassen — both "to wash" and "zich wassen" — to wash oneself). The reflexive pronoun comes immediately after the verb in second position in a sentence, and after the subject in a subordinate clause. In the perfect tense (past tense), reflexive verbs are always conjugated with the auxiliary verb "hebben", not with "zijn". In the imperative mood, the pronoun corresponding to the subject "je/jij" usually remains "je", but with formal "u", "zich" or "u" can be used.

'zich' is used only in the 3rd singular and 3rd plural persons and in the polite 'u' form; in other persons, the corresponding simple pronoun (me, je, ons) is used.

indirect-speech.intro_tr: Indirect speech (indirecte rede) allows us to convey what someone else has said or asked within our own sentence; in Dutch this is usually constructed with a subordinate clause with the conjunction dat or of. Statement clauses are reported with "dat", yes/no questions with "of", and questions with question words are reported with their own question words (wie, wat, waar, wanneer...). Because it is a subordinate clause, the conjugated verb always goes at the end of the sentence (the verb-final rule). If the main verb (zei, vroeg, dacht) is in the past tense, the tense of the reported clause also generally shifts back by one level (present tense → past tense, perfectum → plusquamperfectum, future → zou+infinitive). Additionally, personal pronouns (ik→hij/zij) and temporal/locational adverbs (vandaag→die dag, hier→daar) change according to the perspective.

imperative-mood.intro_tr: In Dutch, the imperative mood (gebiedende wijs) is used to tell someone to do something, to request, or to warn. Its greatest advantage: in most verbs, the imperative mood is the same as the present tense form of "ik" (I) — that is, the verb root/stem — and does not change according to person — the same form is always used for "jij", "jullie" or "u". Only the verb "zijn" (to be) is irregular and becomes "wees". Polite/formal imperatives are generally softened with question patterns like "wilt u..." or "kunt u...". On this page, the formation of the imperative mood, negative imperatives, usage with separable verbs, and the "we" imperative (laten we) are summarized in table form.

conditional.intro_tr: In Dutch, conditional sentences are typically constructed with the conjunction "als" (if) and divided into three main types: real/possible condition (with present tense), weak or hypothetical condition (imperfectum + zou), and unfulfilled condition in the past (plusquamperfectum + zou hebben/zijn + V3). The verb "zou/zouden" corresponds to the Turkish "-se/-sa...-irdi" structure and expresses the result of the conditional sentence. In the subordinate clause, the verb always goes to the end of the sentence; if the subordinate clause beginning with "als" comes first, inverted word order (verb-subject) is used in the main clause. "Als" can sometimes be completely omitted and the subordinate clause can be constructed with inversion (like "Were I rich..." in English); in this case the meaning remains the same but the style is more formal/literary. "Zou" is also frequently used independently of the condition to express politeness, conjecture, and requests.

conjunctions.title_tr: Conjunctions: Main and Subordinate Clause Word Order (want / omdat)
conjunctions.intro_tr: In Dutch, conjunctions are divided into two major groups and each group affects word order within the sentence differently: coordinating conjunctions (nevenschikkend: en, maar, want, of, dus) leave the sentence in normal main clause word order (V2), while subordinating conjunctions (onderschikkend: omdat, dat, als, terwijl, hoewel...) move the verb to the very end of the subordinate clause. The most commonly confused pair is 'want' and 'omdat' — both mean 'because' but one requires straight word order, the other requires verb-final word order. Learning this difference correctly is the key to speaking fluently and correctly at B1 level. The tables below contain all important conjunctions, word order rules, and a want/omdat comparison.

tables.caption_tr: Conjunction Types: General Comparison

footnotes_tr: V2 rule: In main clauses, the conjugated verb appears as the second element (the subject may be in 1st position or another element may be in 1st position).
In subordinate clauses, the verb is moved to the end; in compound tenses, the auxiliary verb also goes to the end with the main verb (e.g., 'omdat hij dat gedaan heeft').

pluperfect.title_tr: Plusquamperfectum (had gedaan) — The Past of the Past
pluperfect.intro_tr: Plusquamperfectum (the past of the miş-form/"had gedaan") is used to describe an action completed BEFORE a specific moment in the past — in other words, it is "the past of the past". In terms of structure, it consists of the imperfectum form (had/hadden or was/waren) of the auxiliary verb hebben or zijn + the voltooid deelwoord (past participle) form of the verb. It largely overlaps with the "-mıştı/-müştü" suffix in Turkish: such as "gitmiştim, yemiştik". Which auxiliary verb (hebben or zijn) will be used is exactly the same as with perfectum (voltooid tegenwoordige tijd). It is typically used in sentences constructed with conjunctions such as voordat, nadat, toen to clarify the sequence of two past events.

men-formal-subjects.intro_tr: "men" is used in Dutch as an impersonal/general subject; it corresponds to the Turkish "insan" (one/people), "kişi" (person) expressions or the passive voice ("...-ılır/-ilir") and is generally found in formal, written, or institutional texts (signs, regulations, newspapers). "u" is a formal "siz" (you) pronoun that conveys politeness; it is used to address both a single person and multiple people with respect, and has its own specific rule in verb conjugation. These two structures are generally taught together at the B2 level for understanding and producing formal Dutch texts. The tables below contain the conjugation, usage areas, and comparison with everyday alternatives for both.

discourse-particles.title_tr: Discourse Particles: toch, wel, maar, eens, even
discourse-particles.intro_tr: In Dutch, discourse particles like "toch, wel, maar, eens, even" (modale partikels) do not change the dictionary meaning of the sentence; instead, they add the speaker's attitude, tone, expectation, or emotion — such as surprise, insistence, reassurance, impatience. These particles generally come right after the conjugated verb and often cannot be translated one-to-one into Turkish; they are conveyed with suffixes like "değil mi", "hele", "bir", "hadi", "bari" or through intonation. They are extremely common in spoken language and are indispensable for natural, fluent Dutch; when used insufficiently, the sentence sounds bookish and cold. On this page, the basic function of each particle, the combinations they are used with, their nuances according to sentence type, and frequently confused distinctions are summarized in table form.

negation-advanced.intro_tr: In Dutch, besides niet and geen, there are also words that express more formal and nuanced negation: nauwelijks (hardly), geenszins (by no means), evenmin (neither), allerminst and noch...noch structures. Since these words already carry negative meaning within themselves, they are not used together with niet or geen — otherwise a double negation error occurs. Some of them (evenmin, nauwelijks) require inverted word order (verb-subject order) when placed at the beginning of a sentence due to Dutch's V2 rule. These structures appear especially frequently in written and formal language, newspaper texts, and literary narrative; at B2 level, it is important to recognize them and place them correctly.

comparative-clauses.intro_tr: In Dutch, three basic structures are used to establish a comparison between two situations or qualities: "hoe...hoe" (how much...that much) expresses proportional increase, "alsof" (as if, supposedly) creates a comparison that is not real or hypothetical, "zoals" (like, as) describes an action or example by likening it to something else. The word order of these three structures differs from each other: hoe...hoe and zoals usually use subordinate clause word order (verb at the end), while alsof always requires subordinate clause word order and indicates whether the sentence is real or not through tense/mood selection. For Turkish speakers, these three structures are frequently confused with the word "gibi", which is why it is important to understand the distinctions in meaning and word order. This page summarizes the rules, exceptions, and frequently confused points of each structure in table form.

tables.caption_tr: Overview of Three Comparison Structures
rows: 'ne kadar...o kadar' — iki değişkenin orantılı artış/azalışı

Yan cümle dizilişi; fiil kümesi cümle sonunda
'gibi, ...dığı gibi' — bir eylemi/durumu başka birine benzetme veya örnekleme
Yan cümle dizilişi (fiil sonda) veya sadece isim öbeği (fiil yok)

passive-tenses.intro_tr: In Dutch, passive voice (lijdende vorm/passief) is constructed with the verb "worden", but which auxiliary verb will be used depends on the tense — this is the point that Turkish students find most confusing. In present and past tense "worden/werden" is used, but in the perfect and pluperfect surprisingly it shifts to the auxiliary verb "zijn" (not worden!). On this page you will find in tabular form the complete conjugations of the six basic tenses of passive voice, their combination with modal verbs, and their comparison with active sentences. Goal: to never mix up structures like "wordt gedaan", "werd gedaan", "is gedaan", and to automatically remember which auxiliary verb comes in which tense.

nominalization.title_tr: Verb Nominalization: het + Infinitive and -ing Suffixes
nominalization.intro_tr: In Dutch, there are two basic ways to convert a verb to a noun (nominalisatie): (1) using the uninflected form of the verb (infinitive) directly with the 'het' article as if it were a noun — this method can be derived from every verb and expresses the action itself, its process; (2) deriving a new noun with a concrete, often result- or institution-referring meaning by adding the '-ing' suffix to the verb root — these nouns always take the 'de' article. The het + infinitive structure is especially frequently used after prepositions (na, tijdens, bij, voor het + infinitive) and corresponds to noun-verbs formed with the Turkish suffixes '-mak/-mek' or '-ma/-me'. The -ing nouns, on the other hand, are similar to '-tion/-ing' ending nouns in English and are usually found as separate entries in dictionaries. These two structures cannot always substitute for each other; meaning and usage context determine the choice.

It has no plural form; it expresses the action itself, the abstract process.

tables.caption_tr: 2. Nominalization with -ing Suffix (Concrete/Result-Meaning Nouns)
footnotes_tr: The -ing nouns always take the 'de' article and their plural is formed with -en (de vertalingen, de beslissingen).
This structure is not productive; not every verb can form a -ing noun, it is necessary to check whether it is registered in the dictionary.

participle-adjectives.intro_tr: In Dutch, both the present participle (tegenwoordig deelwoord: -end) and the past participle (voltooid deelwoord: ge-...-d/-t/-en) can be used as adjectives by appearing directly before a noun; similar to Turkish constructions like "read/read newspaper" or "crying child". The present participle carries an active meaning of the one performing the action itself (huilend kind = crying child), while the past participle carries a completed/passive meaning of the one experiencing the action (gebroken been = broken leg). These participles in adjectival position are subject to the -e addition rule like normal adjectives; however, the past participles of strong (onregelmatig) verbs ending in -en never take the additional -e. Furthermore, many participles have become independent adjectives over time and have acquired a permanent meaning different from the original verb (vermoeiend = tiring, vermoeid = tired).

tables.caption_tr: Formation and Adjective Usage of the Present Participle (Tegenwoordig Deelwoord)
footnotes_tr: The rule is always the same: verb root (stam) + -end. After this suffix, the normal adjective inflection rule (-e ending) is applied.
The present participles of some verbs are rarely used as adjectives (e.g., zijnde, hebbend); these are more commonly seen in formal/written language.

tables.caption_tr: Formation and Adjective Usage of the Past Participle (Voltooid Deelwoord)
footnotes_tr: The participle of regular verbs ends in ge-...-d or ge-...-t and is subject to the normal adjective inflection rule.
The participle of irregular (strong) verbs mostly ends in ge-...-en; this form never takes the additional -e (see table below).

tables.caption_tr: Is the -e Suffix Added to Participles in Adjective Position? (Critical Rule)
rows: Normal sıfat kuralı: -e eklenir, het-woord + belirsiz + tekilde eklenmez
Normal sıfat kuralı: -e eklenir, het-woord + belirsiz + tekilde eklenmez
DEĞİŞMEZ — -en ile biten ortaçlar hiçbir zaman ek -e almaz
footnotes_tr: This rule is based on the same logic as material adjectives ending in -en (houten, gouden, etc.): adjectives ending in -en do not take inflection.
In plural nouns, the de-woord/het-woord distinction disappears; in all plurals, normal participles take -e, but those ending in -en remain unchanged.

tables.caption_tr: Participle Adjectives Derived from Frequently Used Irregular (Strong) Verbs
footnotes_tr: Since all participles in this table end in -en, when used as adjectives they remain unchanged regardless of de-woord/het-woord or definiteness distinction.

tables.caption_tr: Semantic Difference Between Present Participle (Active/Doing) and Past Participle (Passive/Done)
footnotes_tr: The present participle defines the entity CREATING/PERFORMING that characteristic; the past participle, on the other hand, defines the entity EXPERIENCING/UNDERGOING that action.

tables.caption_tr: Permanent Adjectivized Participle Pairs (Similar to English -ing/-ed Adjectives)
footnotes_tr: These pairs are now perceived as independent adjectives in everyday language and have moved away from the original verb meaning — similar to the distinction between 'tiring/tired' in Turkish.
*interessant is historically a loan from French and is not a true Dutch participle; it has been added for comparison purposes.

preposition-nuance.title_tr: Subtle Preposition Distinctions: op / aan / bij / tegen
preposition-nuance.intro_tr: Because the prepositions op, aan, bij, and tegen in Dutch are often expressed in Turkish by the same words ("-de, -e, yanında, karşı"), Turkish students frequently confuse these four prepositions with each other. Yet each has a different type of contact, mode of orientation, and abstract usage domain: op denotes full contact on a flat surface or an abstract "orientation toward," aan denotes partial contact held from an edge/tip or a mental-emotional bond, bij denotes spatial or institutional proximity, and tegen denotes physical contact/support or intellectual opposition. On this page, the basic meanings of the four prepositions, the points where they are most frequently confused with one another, and their use in fixed temporal and idiomatic expressions are summarized in comparative tables. The goal is not so much memorization but answering the question "what contact/orientation logic applies in which situation."

tables.caption_tr: Table 1 — op / aan / bij / tegen: Basic Meanings and Functions

footnotes_tr: These four prepositions are often part of fixed verb patterns; meaning is usually determined together with the verb and cannot be extracted from the preposition alone.

tables.caption_tr: Table 3 — Nuanced Differences Between bij and tegen

relative-advanced.title_tr: Advanced Relative Clauses: wie, hetgeen, waar+edat
relative-advanced.intro_tr: Advanced-level relative clauses come into play when the basic die/dat/waar structure is insufficient: when describing an indefinite or general person, "wie" is used, when referring to an entire clause or situation, "hetgeen" is used, and when connecting objects together with prepositions, the combined forms "waar+edat" are used. These structures appear especially frequently in formal written language and literary style; in everyday speech there are also some simplified alternatives. "Wie" can also carry possessive meaning in the forms "wiens/wier". On this page you will systematically see which relative pronoun each antecedent (person, thing, entire clause) requires.

tables.caption_tr: "wie" and its possessive forms "wiens / wier" usage

Resmî/yazılı dilde kişi + edat kombinasyonunda "die" yerine "edat + wie" tercih edilir
De persoon die ik het boek aan gaf...
Günlük konuşmada edat cümle sonuna atılır, "wie" kullanılmayabilir

"wiens" eril/nötr tekil ve tüm çoğul öncüller için kullanılır
De vrouw wier tas gestolen was...
"wier" dişil tekil için kullanılır, günümüzde çok resmî/edebî, günlük dilde "van wie" tercih edilir
Wie niet waagt, wie niet wint.
"Cesaret etmeyen kazanamaz" — "wie" ile başlayan pek çok Hollandaca atasözü vardır

Günlük konuşma ve yazı dilinde en yaygın

footnotes_tr: "hetgeen" and "wat" can be used interchangeably; "hetgeen" is a more formal and written choice, almost never used in everyday speech.

inseparable-prefixes.intro_tr: In Dutch, the prefixes be-, ver-, ont-, and her- are inseparable prefixes (non-scheidbaar) that create new meanings when added to verbs but are NEVER separated from the verb root. Unlike separable prefixes (op-, aan-, mee-, and similar), these four prefixes are always unstressed and are not stripped from the beginning of the verb and moved to the end in the sentence. The most critical rule for these prefixes is this: in the voltooid deelwoord (perfectum) form of these verbs, the ge- prefix is NEVER used—because the verb already begins with an unstressed prefix. Each prefix has its own semantic inclination: be- generally makes a verb transitive/object-oriented, ver- indicates change or transformation, ont- expresses moving away or the emergence of something, and her- expresses repetition. The tables below contain, for each prefix, its functions, frequently used verbs, the perfect rule, and comparisons with separable verbs.

Değişim, dönüşüm, tamamlanma; bazen olumsuz/yanlış anlam
Uzaklaşma, kaçış, olumsuzlama, bir şeyin ortaya çıkması/başlaması
footnotes_tr: Besides these four prefixes, ge- and mis- also belong to the inseparable prefix group, but this page focuses on be-, ver-, ont-, and her-.

ge- önek ile kök arasına girer

word-order-inversion.intro_tr: In Dutch, in a normal sentence the subject comes before the verb (Ik ga naar huis), but when an element other than the subject (temporal/locational/manner adverb, prepositional phrase, subordinate clause, object, quotation, etc.) is placed at the beginning of the sentence, the conjugated verb and subject swap positions; this is called "inverted word order" (inversie). This rule is a direct consequence of Dutch's fundamental V2 (verb-second) principle: the conjugated verb must always remain in the second position in the main clause regardless — if the subject is in the first position, straight word order results, if another element is placed first, inverted word order emerges. Inverted word order is not only a mandatory grammatical rule but also a way of emphasizing a particular element (time, place, negation, object) by placing it at the beginning of the sentence. While conjunctions like "en, maar, want, of, dus (in conjunction sense)" do not trigger inverted word order, adverbial conjunctions like "daarom, toch, dus (in adverbial sense), daarna, echter" always require inverted word order; not knowing this distinction is one of the most frequent mistakes made by students at B1-B2 level.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Rule: Normal Word Order vs. Inverted Word Order (Within the V2 Framework)
rows: Cümle başında özne var; fiil zaten 2. sırada, devrik diziliş yok.
Zaman zarfı 'morgen' başa alınınca özne ile fiil yer değiştirir, fiil yine 2. sırada kalır.
Als het regent, blijf ik thuis.
Bütün yan cümle tek bir 'öğe' sayılır; ana cümlede fiil-özne yer değiştirir.
Nesne vurgu amacıyla öne alınır; fiil yine ikinci sırada kalmak zorundadır.
Yer belirten edat öbeği başa gelince özne-fiil devrik olur.
footnotes_tr: Golden rule: The conjugated verb is ALWAYS the second element in the main clause; if the first element is not the subject, the subject moves immediately AFTER the verb.

tables.caption_tr: Types of Elements That Trigger Inversion
rows: In de kast staan de glazen.
Die film heb ik al gezien.
Toen ik klein was, woonde ik in Rotterdam.
Daarom heb ik het niet gedaan.

tables.caption_tr: Conjunctions/Adverbs That Require and Do Not Require Inversion (Frequently Confused Distinction)

Soru kelimesi 1. öğe, fiil yine 2. sırada.
Ik weet niet of hij komt.

infinitive-clusters.title_tr: Verb Clusters: laten, zien, horen + Infinitive
infinitive-clusters.intro_tr: In Dutch, when laten, zien, horen (and similar verbs like voelen, helpen) are used together with an infinitive, the second verb is not conjugated and a "verb cluster" (werkwoordcluster) is formed at the end of the sentence. laten basically carries the meaning of "to make, to cause, to let," while zien and horen are perception verbs and convey the meaning of "someone/something being seen/heard performing an action." The most important feature of these verbs is that in compound tenses (perfectum, plusquamperfectum), the infinitive form is used again instead of the normal past participle (voltooid deelwoord) — this is called the IPP rule (Infinitivus Pro Participio / "Infinitive in Place of Participle"). In three-verb clusters (auxiliary verb + laten/zien/horen + infinitive), there are specific word order patterns both in the main clause and in the subordinate clause, and in the subordinate clause two different arrangements called "red order" and "green order" (rode volgorde and groene volgorde) are possible. This page presents the basic structure, the IPP rule, syntax patterns, and frequently used idiomatic combinations in systematic tables.

tables.caption_tr: General Structure: laten, zien, horen (+ voelen, helpen) + Infinitive
footnotes_tr: The object (accusative/lijdend voorwerp) always comes before the infinitive: laten/zien/horen + OBJECT + INFINITIVE.
The infinitive following these verbs does not take 'te': 'zien lopen' (correct), 'zien te lopen' (incorrect).

tables.caption_tr: IPP Rule (Infinitivus Pro Participio) — Infinitive Use in Perfectum
rows: Ik heb hem zien lopen. (gezien DEĞİL)
Ik heb haar horen zingen. (gehoord DEĞİL)
Hij heeft het laten repareren. (gelaten DEĞİL)
Ik heb het voelen gebeuren. (gevoeld DEĞİL)
Ona taşınmasında yardım ettim. (İki biçim de kabul edilir)
footnotes_tr: The IPP rule applies to verbs used together with an infinitive, such as laten, zien, horen, voelen, helpen, and modal verbs (kunnen, moeten, willen, etc.).
helpen is an exception: both 'geholpen' and 'helpen' (IPP) are acceptable, but the IPP form is more common.

tables.caption_tr: Syntax: Verb Cluster Word Order (Main Clause and Subordinate Clause)
rows: Yan cümle (3 fiilli, kırmızı sıra — yaygın/standart)
Yan cümle (3 fiilli, yeşil sıra — alternatif/Flaman)
footnotes_tr: 'Red order' (rode volgorde) is more common in standard written Dutch in the Netherlands.
'Green order' (groene volgorde) is particularly common in Belgian Flemish and in spoken language.

tables.caption_tr: Frequently Used Patterns and Idiomatic Combinations

Ze laat het doen door een expert.
Ik heb mijn tas laten liggen.

tables.caption_tr: Special Uses of laten: Permission, Causality, Passive Meaning, and Exhortation
footnotes_tr: The 'Laten we' pattern functions as a command/exhortation for the 1st person plural in formal speech and writing; this construction is also related to the topic of 'Frozen Subjunctive Mood.'
The 'zich laten + infinitive' construction carries a passive-potential meaning close to the English 'can be done.'

conditional-perfect.title_tr: Past Conditional (zou hebben gedaan) — Unrealized Past Assumptions
conditional-perfect.intro_tr: The "zou hebben gedaan" construction is used to describe hypothetical situations that did not occur in the past and corresponds to Turkish expressions like "yapmış olurdum", "gitmiş olurdum". The pattern is formed as zou/zouden + hebben/zijn + past participle and is usually seen together with a conditional clause starting with als and containing a pluperfect (had gedaan) — because both the condition and the result remained in the past, an unrealized possibility. This structure is important at the B2 level because it parallels the English "would have done" pattern and carries meanings of regret, assumption, and "if only" directed at the past. Whether hebben or zijn is used is determined according to the normal perfectum/pluperfectum rules. Additionally, both "zou hebben gedaan" and "zou gedaan hebben" word orders are valid; the latter is more common in spoken language.

laten-causative.intro_tr: The verb "Laten" is used to express causative (causative) structures in Turkish and carries the meanings of "to make someone do something" or "to allow someone to do something". It is constructed with the pattern "Laten" + infinitive (infinitief); that is, "Laten" is conjugated, while the second verb remains in the infinitive form at the end of the sentence. This structure can encompass both "causation" (making someone do work, e.g., getting a haircut from a hairdresser) and "permission" (letting, allowing) meanings; context determines the meaning. "Laten" is also part of a broad verb cluster family used together with perception verbs like "zien", "horen", "voelen" (verb clusters/werkwoordelijke groep) and in compound tenses (perfectum, plusquamperfectum) it is subject to a special "double infinitive" (dubbele infinitief / IPP-effect) rule.

er-advanced.title_tr: Advanced Uses of er: Partial er and er as Passive Subject
er-advanced.intro_tr: The two most confusing advanced uses of the word "Er": (1) partial er (partitief er) — after a quantity word (twee, veel, weinig, genoeg, een paar), it takes the place of a previously mentioned noun, giving the meaning of "from it/from them"; (2) as a temporary subject in passive sentences — if the true subject (logical subject) is not at the beginning of the sentence, it is used to start the sentence in worden/zijn passive constructions, and it has no real meaning, serving only as a grammatical placeholder. These two uses are completely different from each other, but because both share the same word form of "er", students often confuse them. On this page, we examine both separately, with their rules and examples.

cleft-sentences.intro_tr: A cleft sentence (in Dutch, "gespleten zin") is an advanced syntactic structure used to split a sentence's normal element into two parts using the pattern "het is/was ... die/dat ..." in order to emphasize that element strongly. It has a function similar to Turkish structures like "...-dır, ...-en/-an" or "the one who/the thing that ...": the speaker brings forward a piece of information from the sentence (the subject, object, or adverb) and transforms the rest into a relative clause (die/dat). The choice of die/dat, just as in normal relative clauses, is determined by the de-woord/het-woord and singular/plural properties of the emphasized element. This structure appears frequently in written language, especially in contexts of discussion and comparison ("not this, but that"), and tense agreement (is/was/is geweest) is adjusted according to the rest of the sentence.

subjunctive-remnants.title_tr: Fossilized Optative Mood (leve, moge, het zij zo)
subjunctive-remnants.intro_tr: In Dutch, verb conjugation used to have a separate "optative mood" (aanvoegende wijs / conjunctief) form; today this mood is no longer productive, meaning new sentences are not formed with this pattern in everyday speech. However, in frozen (fossilized) fixed expressions like "leve de koning", "het zij zo", "moge het je goed gaan", traces of this old mood still live on. These forms generally carry a sense of wish, desire, curse, blessing, or formal-ceremonial style and use a special form derived from the root, different from present tense mood verb conjugation. At the C1 level it is important to recognize these fixed patterns because they appear frequently in literature, religious texts, anthems, and formal discourse; but when you speak, you are not expected to produce them—it is enough to know their meanings and recognize them.

formal-prepositional-phrases.title_tr: Official Prepositional Phrases (ten aanzien van, met betrekking tot)
formal-prepositional-phrases.intro_tr: In Dutch formal written language (ambtelijk/formeel Nederlands), the simple prepositions used in everyday speech (over, om, door, voor) are replaced by long and fixed prepositional phrases: "ten aanzien van", "met betrekking tot", "met het oog op" and the like. These phrases are usually used together with a noun compound and appear frequently in formal correspondence, legal texts, journalism, and academic language. Although they are very close in meaning to each other, each one is preferred in a specific context (reason, purpose, exception, subject) and they should not be confused. These structures usually appear at the beginning of the sentence, bringing the subject (topic) to the fore, and then the main clause follows the V2 rule. This page presents the most frequently used official prepositional phrases grouped by function, together with their everyday language equivalents.

impersonal-passive.intro_tr: Impersonal passive (onpersoonlijke lijdende vorm), which is formed by putting intransitive verbs that do not take an object (dansen, werken, lachen and the like) into the passive voice; in this structure there is no real subject, only the action itself is emphasized. Since there is no real subject in the sentence, the Dutch rule of "an element must be at the beginning of the sentence" (V2) is satisfied by using "er" as a shadow subject. In the sentence "Er wordt gedanst" (There is dancing), it is not specified who is dancing, only that the action of dancing is taking place. This structure can be formed in all tenses of the worden verb (wordt, werd, is geworden, was geworden). The position of "Er" in the sentence varies depending on whether there is another element at the beginning of the sentence, and sometimes it can be dropped entirely.

te-infinitive-advanced.title_tr: Advanced te + Infinitive Constructions (alvorens te, zonder te)
te-infinitive-advanced.intro_tr: Advanced-level "te + infinitive" structures, used together with prepositions that function as conjunctions (alvorens, zonder, door, na, teneinde, in plaats van, etc.), reduce a subordinate clause to a single infinitive phrase. These patterns can only be constructed when the subject of the main clause and the shortened subordinate clause is THE SAME; if the subjects are different, switching to fully-conjunctive structures such as "zonder dat", "voordat", "nadat", "doordat" is mandatory. In separable verbs, "te" always enters between the separable prefix and the verb root (e.g., "zonder op te bellen"). When reference to the past is needed, the complete infinitive (voltooid infinitief) in the form of "te hebben/zijn + past participle" is used. These structures appear frequently especially in formal, academic, and written Dutch; in everyday speech, simpler conjunctions are generally preferred.

modality-nuance.title_tr: Modality Nuances: schijnen, blijken, lijken, horen te
modality-nuance.intro_tr: In Dutch, the verbs schijnen, blijken, lijken, and horen te/behoren te are subtle modality nuances that express the degree of certainty of a piece of information and its source (evidentiality). schijnen conveys information heard from others with questionable certainty ("according to rumor"); blijken conveys a fact verified by evidence and revealed later ("it turned out that"); lijken conveys the speaker's personal impression/observation ("it seems that"). horen te and its more formal version behoren te carry the meaning of "-meli/-malı" derived from a moral or social norm, and express a softer, etiquette-based obligation than moeten. These four verbs are generally used with the pattern "Subject + verb + te + infinitive" or the pattern "Het + verb + that..."

word-formation.intro_tr: Dutch has a rich suffix system that allows producing many derived words from a limited number of roots. On this page, four productive suffixes are examined: -heid (makes an abstract noun from an adjective, "-lik/-lık"), -baar (makes an adjective expressing "capability" from a verb, "-ebilir"), -lijk (makes an adjective from a noun or verb in the sense of "related to / -like / -ish"), and -achtig (makes a similarity-denoting "-like/similar" adjective from a noun). Each suffix has its own unique phonetic and spelling rules, plural forms (especially -heden for -heid), and lexicalized (i.e., rule-breaking) examples. At C1 level, recognizing these suffixes enables both quick comprehension when reading texts and producing natural words in academic/formal style.

tables.caption_tr: 1. The -heid suffix: deriving abstract nouns from adjectives ("-lik/-lık")
footnotes_tr: In the plural, -heid usually takes the form -heden (the d sound is preserved, as seen in some older inflectional traces like 'stad → steden').
Some adjectives historically take -te instead of -heid (ziekte, hoogte, lengte, breedte); these are exceptions that must be memorized.
Abstract/uncountable -heid nouns (such as gezondheid, duidelijkheid) are generally not pluralized.

tables.caption_tr: 2. The -baar suffix: deriving "capability" adjectives from verbs ("-ebilir/-ılabilir")
footnotes_tr: The -baar suffix cannot be added to every verb; while productive, many forms have become lexicalized (fixed, must be learned by rote).
zichtbaar is derived from an irregular root (zicht) of the verb zien; this kind of root change is not rare for the -baar suffix.
The negative is usually formed with the on- prefix: onbetaalbaar, onleesbaar, onzichtbaar, onbruikbaar.

tables.caption_tr: 3. The -lijk suffix: deriving adjectives from nouns or verbs ("-sel/-like/related to")
footnotes_tr: The -lijk suffix can derive adjectives from both nouns and verb roots; the meaning often varies between 'related to', 'showing' or 'capable'.
Some -lijk derivatives denoting time take the form -lijks as an adverb/adjective: dagelijks, wekelijks, maandelijks, jaarlijks.
The negative is again formed with the on- prefix: onmogelijk, onduidelijk, onvriendelijk, ongevaarlijk (this last form is rare/impractical, 'veilig' is preferred).

tables.caption_tr: 4. The -achtig suffix: deriving similarity/appearance adjectives from nouns ("-like/similar")
footnotes_tr: The -achtig suffix can be added to both nouns (goud, kind) and adjectives (groen, zwart); in the latter case, it gives a sense of color/quality shading.
The -achtig suffix is quite productive and frequently used in everyday speech to create new words (usually translated as 'like' or '-ish').

tables.caption_tr: 5. Summary comparison of the four suffixes
footnotes_tr: All -heid derivatives are always de-words (de eerlijkheid, de veiligheid).
Adjectives are subject to inflection rules within the sentence (see Adjective Inflection -e suffix): een gevaarlijke situatie, het gevaarlijke dier.

tables.caption_tr: 6. Examples of combined use with the on- negation prefix
footnotes_tr: The on- prefix is very productive with adjectives ending in -baar and -lijk; this pattern is less common with -heid and -achtig derivatives.
The combination on- + -heid is also possible but rare: highly complex derivations like onbetrouwbaarheid ('unreliability') are found in formal/written language.

triple-verb-clusters.title_tr: Triple Verb Clusters (zou hebben kunnen doen)
triple-verb-clusters.intro_tr: In Dutch, in some sentences three verbs are arranged consecutively in infinitive form, creating a complex 'verb cluster' (werkwoordcluster): zou/zouden expressing condition, hebben (or zijn) expressing 'possession/completion', a modal verb (kunnen, moeten, willen, mogen, durven), and finally the infinitive form of the main verb. This structure is used to express hypothetical, possible, or necessary situations referring to the past, such as 'would have been able to do' or 'might have done'. The order of verbs in the cluster determines both grammatical correctness and the semantic scope of the sentence (ability or possibility). Furthermore, according to the 'IPP rule' (Ersatzinfinitief), modal verbs used with hebben take the infinitive form instead of the normal past participle (gekund, gemoeten, etc.). Since this topic is an advanced-level structure at C1 level, it is recommended to first know well the topics of Modal Verbs, Past Conditional, and Perfectum.

compound-nouns.intro_tr: In Dutch, compound nouns (samengestelde zelfstandige naamwoorden) are formed by writing two or more words together as a single word, which differs fundamentally from Turkish's separately written noun phrases (e.g. "okul çantası") — in Dutch, connected writing is mandatory (schooltas). The gender (de/het) and plural form of a compound are always determined by the FINAL element, while stress typically falls on the FIRST element. Sometimes between two elements, a "linking sound" (verbindingsklank) appears, coming from historical plurals or old inflectional endings: the most common are -s- and -en-; in some cases no linking sound is used at all. These affixes carry no meaning; they only ease pronunciation and usually originate from the historical plural form of the first word or from certain suffixes (-heid, -ing, -schap, etc.). The rules describe general patterns; many exceptions must be memorized.

text-connectors.intro_tr: Text connectors (tekstconnectoren) are adverbial words that show logical relationships (addition, contrast, result, sequencing) between sentences or paragraphs. Unlike classical conjunctions such as "En, maar, want", words like bovendien, desondanks, daarentegen are grammatically counted as bijwoord (adverbs), and when they come at the beginning of a sentence, they lead to inverted word order (verb-subject) according to Dutch's V2 rule. These connectors are especially used in written and formal/academic texts (C1 level) to clarify relationships between ideas, and they provide a richer, layered style compared to simple conjunctions in spoken language. On this page, connectors are grouped by semantic categories, and the word order (inversion) rule is shown in a separate table.

correlative-conjunctions.intro_tr: Correlative conjunctions (correlatieve voegwoorden) are pairs of conjunctions that link two elements or two clauses to each other, creating a mutual relationship between them such as "both...and", "neither...nor", "either...or". The most frequently used in Dutch are zowel...als (both...and), noch...noch (neither...nor), hetzij...hetzij/of (either...or) and niet alleen...maar (ook) (not only...but also) structures. These structures are generally preferred in formal and written language; simpler alternatives (en...en, of...of) are preferred in everyday conversation. Each conjunction has its own specific rules for negation agreement, verb conjugation, and word order within the sentence; this page focuses on these subtleties.

punctuation-style.intro_tr: Two topics constantly challenge students in Dutch spelling: the tussen-n inserted between compound words (like the -en- in boekenkast'taki) and the apostrophe's use (punctuation mark) in plurals, possessives, and spoken language abbreviations. The tussen-n rule is fundamentally based on the question "does the singular noun form its plural with -en or with -s", but famous exceptions like boomgaard and hoofdpijn must be memorized. The apostrophe, however, is never used in Dutch to show possession in words ending with normal consonants (not Peters; Piet's bag is not "Piets tas" nor "Piet's" — see table); it only comes into play in words ending with vowels and in spoken language abbreviations ('t, 'n, 'k). This page systematizes the official Woordenlijst rules in table form for Turkish-speaking students.

dummy-subjects-advanced.intro_tr: In Dutch, every sentence must have a grammatical subject, but in some sentences there is no real 'subject' in the true sense (weather, time, general statements) or the real subject is indefinite so it cannot be placed at the beginning of the sentence. The words 'het' and 'er' fill this gap; they are called dummy subjects. 'het' usually represents abstract situations without real existence or a subordinate clause/infinitive phrase that comes later, while 'er' represents indefinite, concrete but real subjects that cannot stand at the beginning of the sentence or is used in impersonal passive constructions. At the advanced level, distinguishing these two from each other, when they can be dropped, and the difference between patterns like 'het zijn' / 'er zijn' often causes difficulty for students. This page maps out these subtleties completely at C2 level.

idiomatic-structures.intro_tr: In Dutch, idioms and proverbs (spreekwoorden), are fixed expressions that enrich everyday speech but cannot be translated literally. In these structures, elements such as definiteness, prepositions, possessive pronouns, and even diminutive suffixes are generally FIXED — when altered, the expression becomes meaningless or incorrect. On this page, the most frequently used idioms, proverbs, their grammatical "frozen" characteristics, and typical errors are presented in tabular form. The aim is to memorize these patterns as they are and to be able to use them in the correct context; a word-by-word translation approach does not work here.

literary-tenses.title_tr: Literary Narrative Tenses and Historical Present Tense (Historisch Presens)
literary-tenses.intro_tr: In Dutch literary texts, historical narratives, and journalism, writers frequently shift from standard narrative past (imperfectum) to 'historical present tense' (historisch presens), thereby adding vividness and reality to the narrative. Additionally, in literary narration, 'free indirect discourse' (vrije indirecte rede / erlebte rede) is commonly seen, which conveys the character's thoughts in narrative tense without quotation marks or the 'dat' conjunction. This page systematically addresses which tense is used when and why, the signal words that trigger tense shifts, and narrative techniques (direct, indirect, free indirect). At the C2 level, recognizing these subtleties and reproducing them is critical for advanced reading and writing skills.

ellipsis-gapping.title_tr: Ellipsis and Shared Element Dropping (Ellipsis & Gapping)
ellipsis-gapping.intro_tr: Ellipsis is the omission of elements (verb, subject, noun phrase, subordinate clause, etc.) that can be understood from a previous sentence or context within a sentence, without repeating them. Gapping, on the other hand, is a special type of ellipsis that refers to the deletion of a shared verb from the second sentence in two sentences connected with a conjunction. These structures shorten sentences in Dutch and provide a flowing, formal, and literary style; however, which elements can be omitted is dependent on strict syntactic rules. This is an advanced syntax topic at the C2 level because performing ellipsis correctly requires clearly understanding the complete underlying structure of the sentence (who did what, which tense, which preposition). In the tables below, the types of ellipsis, rules, and common mistakes are summarized systematically.

complex-passive-transforms.intro_tr: Krijgen-passive (krijgen-passief) is, unlike the standard worden-passive in Dutch, a special passive construction that moves the indirect object (recipient/beneficiary) in the sentence to the subject position. The worden-passive, when saying "Het boek wordt gegeven," emphasizes the direct object (the book); krijgen-passive, on the other hand, by saying "Hij krijgt het boek gegeven," brings the recipient (that person) to the forefront. This construction can only be formed with ditransitive verbs—such as geven, sturen, vertellen, beloven—and is conjugated in all tenses; especially in perfectum and plusquamperfectum, a double past participle (gegeven gekregen) appears, and the auxiliary verb is always hebben. Furthermore, sensory-experiential patterns like "te horen krijgen," "te zien krijgen" are a special branch of this family that uses te + infinitive instead of a past participle. At C2 level, being able to construct this form correctly in the right tenses and with the correct past participle sequence brings naturalness to advanced written and spoken expression.

stylistic-inversion.title_tr: Stylistic Inversion and Heavy Constituent Extraposition
stylistic-inversion.intro_tr: Stylistic inversion (stilistische inversie), beyond Dutch's obligatory V2 rule, is the conscious alteration of the order of sentence elements by the author to create emphasis, balance, or narrative effect. Heavy constituent extraposition (extrapositie / zware-constituent-verschuiving), on the other hand, is when long and complex subjects or complements — especially dat/om te/wat subordinate clauses — are moved to the end of the sentence and replaced with a formal placeholder such as het or er. This, in accordance with the "end-weight" principle, makes the text easier to read and understand. These structures appear in written, literary, and formal Dutch rather than everyday speech and require mastery at the C2 level. The purpose is not only grammatical correctness but managing information flow (old information → new information) and stylistic elegance.

archaic-case-remnants.title_tr: Frozen Compounds and Old Inflection Traces (der, des, te allen tijde)
archaic-case-remnants.intro_tr: Modern Dutch names and adjectives no longer change according to case (case) inflection; however, in the language, many frozen compounds from the old Germanic case system (nominative, genitive, dative, accusative cases) still remain. These appear especially in formal written language, legal texts, religious texts, proverbs, and some adverbial/preposition phrases: old definiteness forms like "der", "des", "ter", "ten" and genitive -s remnants like "'s ochtends". These structures are no longer productive, meaning they cannot be used freely when constructing new sentences — they are only fixed expressions that must be memorized. At C2 level, recognizing these compounds, understanding literary texts and formal language correctly is necessary; in daily conversation, their place is taken by modern preposition phrases like "van de", "aan de", "in het".

'der' is used as feminine singular and genitive plural for all genders — for this reason it appears in compounds like 'der Nederlanden' (Dutch territories).

nominal-style.intro_tr: Ambtelijk taalgebruik (nominalized official style), seen in Dutch in official correspondence, legal texts, regulations, and institutional language; a heavy and distant form of writing in which verbs are not used directly but are transformed into nouns and used together with a "carrier" (light) verb. For example, in everyday language "wij voeren het uit" (we implement) is replaced with "de uitvoering vindt plaats" (implementation takes place) in official texts. This style is based on deriving nouns from verbs using suffixes like -ing, -atie, -heid, -sel, or the "het + infinitive" pattern, as well as on official prepositional phrases like "met betrekking tot", "ten aanzien van". At C2 level, recognizing this structure is necessary for correctly understanding official texts (municipal writings, contracts, laws) and producing them when needed; excessive use in everyday conversation, however, is perceived as affected and heavy in style.

flemish-differences.title_tr: Belgian Flemish Differences (gij, ge, word choice)
flemish-differences.intro_tr: Belgian Flemish (Vlaams) differs noticeably from Standard Dutch (Standaardnederlands) spoken in the Netherlands in pronunciation, word choice, and certain grammatical points. The most striking difference is that the historical 'gij/ge' forms are still actively used in everyday and even semi-formal speech as the second person singular pronoun, instead of 'jij/je'. Additionally, Belgian Flemish contains many words borrowed from French (frigo, camion, goesting, etc.) and so-called "false friends"—words that carry different meanings in the two variants (schoon, tas, etc.). This page presents, with the aim of building C2-level literary/discursive awareness, personal pronoun inflections, verb-subject agreement, word choice, and politeness formulas in comparative tables. Note: This is not a dialect but is recognized as 'Belgian Dutch' (Belgisch Nederlands) with its own norms, and in formal writing it generally approximates Standard Dutch.
