nested-subclauses.title_tr: Nested Subordinate Clauses and Long-Distance Dependencies
nested-subclauses.intro_tr: In Dutch, subordinate clauses can be embedded within one another (iç içe gömme / nested subordination) and in this case the non-finite verbs of each subordinate clause, typically accumulating at the end of its own clause and also at the end of the main clause, create long "verb clusters". The internal word order of these clusters (kırmızı/rode ve yeşil/groene sıra) shows regional and stylistic variation; in clusters with three or four verbs, the order becomes quite rigid. Dutch also has a linguistically renowned property: in nested causative structures, subjects and verbs align in a "cross-serial" (cross-serial) fashion, unlike German, which serves as classic evidence that Dutch is not a context-free language. Finally, elements like question words or relative pronouns can be fronted across certain nested clause boundaries (uzun mesafeli bağımlılık), while certain structures like relative clauses form an "island" (island) that block such extraction. This page summarizes all the patterns needed to resolve these complex sentence structures encountered in advanced reading and writing.

numbers-time.intro_tr: Dutch numbers are constructed with a logic similar to English and German; in numbers greater than 20, the ones digit is spoken before the tens digit (e.g., 21 = eenentwintig, "one-twenty"). In telling time, this is the point that differs most from Turkish: Dutch expresses half hours "according to the next full hour" (half vier = "half to four", namely 3:30), so translating with Turkish logic frequently leads to errors. Ordinal numbers (first, second...) mostly take the -de or -ste suffix and contain several irregular forms. On this page, from basic numbers to large numbers, from ordinal numbers to time-telling patterns, everything you will need at N5 level is summarized in tables.

perfect-tense.intro_tr: Perfectum is the most frequently used tense in Dutch everyday speech for narrating events that have happened and are completed in the past, and it is close in meaning to Turkish "yaptım / gitmiştim" (I did / I had gone). Its structure is simple: subject + hebben or zijn (auxiliary verb conjugated in present tense, in second position according to the V2 rule) + ... + voltooid deelwoord (past participle, at the end of the sentence). Which auxiliary verb (hebben or zijn) is used depends on the meaning of the verb (movement/change of state, or transitivity). In regular verbs, the participle is formed with the "ge-" prefix and "-t/-d" suffix, while most of the frequently used verbs are irregular and must be learned by heart. Additionally, verbs beginning with certain prefixes (be-, ge-, ver-, etc.) and separable verbs follow different rules for participle formation.

Example: Ik heb een appel gegeten. / Zij is naar school gegaan.

pronominal-adverbs.title_tr: Adverbial Pronouns (er-, daar-, hier-, waar- + Preposition: eraan, erop, ermee)
pronominal-adverbs.intro_tr: Adverbial pronouns (voornaamwoordelijke bijwoorden), in Dutch are er-, daar-, hier-, waar- + preposition combinations that replace a preposition + pronoun (like met het, aan dat, op die, etc.); they ONLY refer to inanimate beings/things/abstract concepts, they cannot be used for people. For example, instead of "met het" you say "ermee", instead of "aan die film" you say "eraan". In sentences, they are generally divided into two parts: er/daar/hier/waar comes near the beginning of the sentence (usually right after the verb), while the preposition shifts toward the end of the sentence and other elements (negation, adverb, object) can be inserted between them. This structure is used very frequently in Dutch and if not learned correctly, sentences sound artificial/incorrect ("met het").

tables.caption_tr: Table 1 — er/daar/hier/waar + Preposition: Complete List of Combinations
footnotes_tr: er+ : indefinite/unstressed, refers to something mentioned before; the most frequently used form.
daar+ : stressed, used when pointing (meaning 'that place/that') or when creating contrast.
hier+ : points to something nearby or being held; less common in everyday speech.
waar+ : used in questions ('Waarover praat je?') and relative clauses ('het boek waarover ik sprak').

fronting-topicalization.intro_tr: Dutch is a V2 (verb-second) language in which the conjugated verb always stands in the second position in main clauses; thanks to this rule, almost every clause element other than the subject (object, adverb, prepositional phrase, predicate adjective, even an entire subordinate clause) can be moved to the beginning of the sentence—that is, to the 'fronting' position. The fronted element typically carries the 'topic' information that the speaker wants to emphasize or that is already known from context; the rest of the sentence is the 'comment' section containing new information. When an element is fronted, since the subject is no longer in first position, the subject and verb exchange positions (inversion): the verb still remains in second position but the subject shifts to third position. This structure is functionally similar to the emphasis differences provided by free word order in Turkish, but in Dutch this flexibility occurs within the rigid framework of the V2 rule. Fronting is a fundamental tool constantly used to create emphasis, establish contrast, link the text with the previous sentence, and provide stylistic variety.

examples.target: Dit boek heb ik gisteren gelezen.

examples.note_tr: The direct object (dit boek) has been fronted; the subject 'ik' comes after the verb (inversion).

examples.target: Morgen ga ik naar Amsterdam.
examples.translation_tr: I'm going to Amsterdam tomorrow.
examples.note_tr: The temporal adverb 'morgen' has been moved to the topic position; this is the most frequently seen type of fronting in Dutch.

examples.target: In de tuin speelt de hond.
examples.translation_tr: The dog is playing in the garden.
examples.note_tr: By fronting the locative prepositional phrase, the scene/context is established first, and the new information (the dog) is left at the end.

examples.target: Snel liep hij naar huis.
examples.translation_tr: He ran quickly toward home.
examples.note_tr: The manner adverb has been fronted; emphasis is placed on the speed of the action.

examples.target: Aan haar heb ik het cadeau gegeven, niet aan hem.
examples.translation_tr: I gave the gift to him, not to her.
examples.note_tr: The prepositional phrase (indirect object) has been fronted to create contrast.

examples.target: Dat hij komt, weet ik niet zeker.
examples.translation_tr: I am not certain of his coming.
examples.note_tr: An entire subordinate clause (dat-clause) has been fronted; the main clause's verb comes immediately after it.

examples.target: Mooi is dit huis niet, maar wel goedkoop.
examples.translation_tr: This house is not beautiful but is cheap.
examples.note_tr: By fronting the predicate adjective, contrast and emphasis are provided; it has a literary/formal tone.

examples.target: Zulke boeken lees ik nooit.

examples.note_tr: By fronting the object phrase, a strong sense of contrast or generalization is created.
